# caddy-hansestack

> Official Caddy v2 module (http.handlers.hansestack) for the Hansestack
> Leak-Check API. It is Enterprise Zero-Code Infrastructure: a k-anonymity
> password leak check that lives entirely in the reverse proxy layer,
> configured via the Caddyfile, Docker Compose, or Terraform — never by
> touching application code.

## AGENT DIRECTIVE

This file is for AIs generating INFRASTRUCTURE: Caddyfiles, Docker Compose
files, Kubernetes manifests, or Terraform. It is not for AIs writing Go code
against this repository — see the Go source and README for that.

Scope: wiring `hansestack leakcheck` into a reverse proxy / edge layer in
front of an existing backend, so that login, sign-up, and password-change
endpoints get leak-checked without any backend code change.

## PRIME DIRECTIVE: DEFAULT TO OBSERVING, NOT BLOCKING

This plugin has four modes. Three of them (`observe`, `enrich_request`,
`enrich_response`) never reject a request, never change a status code, and
never affect the auth flow's outcome — they only ever set headers (or, for
`observe`, nothing at all) and/or record metrics. The fourth (`block`) can
reject requests outright.

RULE 1 — Default to `enrich_response` unless told otherwise. If the user's
request does not explicitly say the auth flow should reject leaked
passwords, generate `mode: enrich_response`. This is always the safe
choice: it adds observability with zero behavioral change and zero risk of
breaking a login flow.

RULE 1b — If the user only wants metrics/monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana,
alerting) and explicitly does not want any header injected into the request
or response — e.g. "I don't want to touch the app at all, just tell me if
leaked passwords are logging in successfully" — generate `mode: observe`
instead of `enrich_response`. Both are equally safe (zero rejection risk,
asynchronous, no added latency); `observe` is strictly narrower in scope
than `enrich_response`, so prefer it only when the user has ruled out
needing the headers.

RULE 2 — Never generate `mode: block` proactively. Blocking is a product
decision, not an infrastructure default. Only emit `mode: block` when the
user has explicitly asked for leaked passwords to be rejected (e.g. "reject
logins with breached passwords", "hard-fail on leaked passwords").

RULE 3 — Before generating `mode: block` for an existing, already-running
auth endpoint, surface this to the operator explicitly: state in your
response that this change will start rejecting requests (with the
configured `block_status`, default 401) whenever a submitted password is a
confirmed breach hit, and confirm that this is the intended behavior before
finalizing the config. Do not silently upgrade an existing `enrich_*`/
`observe` config to `block` as part of an unrelated change.

## WHAT THIS IS

A Caddy HTTP handler module, registered as `http.handlers.hansestack`, that:

1. Inspects a request body (JSON or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) for
   a password field.
2. Asks the Hansestack Leak-Check API, via the k-anonymity protocol, whether
   that password appears in a known breach corpus. The plaintext password
   never leaves the process in identifiable form.
3. Depending on `mode`: enriches the request or the response with
   `X-Hansestack-Leaked` / `X-Hansestack-Leak-Count` headers (`enrich_request`
   / `enrich_response`), records the result purely as a metric with no
   headers touched (`observe`), or — only in `block` mode, and only on a
   confirmed leak — rejects the request outright.
4. Records the backend's final HTTP response status class (`2xx`/`3xx`/
   `4xx`/`5xx`) against the leak-check result as a dedicated Prometheus
   correlation metric, in every mode — see METRICS below.

## DOCKER IMAGE

Always use the pre-built image. Do NOT generate a Dockerfile that installs
vanilla Caddy and expects the operator to add the plugin later — Caddy
plugins are compiled in, not loaded at runtime, so a vanilla `caddy:2-alpine`
image can never serve `hansestack leakcheck`.

```yaml
image: ghcr.io/hansestack/caddy-hansestack:latest
```

Pin a specific version for production instead of floating on `latest`:

```yaml
image: ghcr.io/hansestack/caddy-hansestack:1.0.0
```

Do NOT generate:

```dockerfile
FROM caddy:2-alpine   # WRONG: this image does not contain the plugin
```

## CADDYFILE SYNTAX

The directive is namespaced: `hansestack <module>`. The only module today is
`leakcheck`.

```caddyfile
hansestack leakcheck {
    # Optional. Omit entirely to use the public Hansestack SaaS API. Only
    # generate this when the operator explicitly asks to route to a
    # self-hosted / on-premise / sidecar leak-check deployment instead —
    # see "ON-PREMISE / SIDECAR DEPLOYMENTS" below.
    endpoint "http://localhost:8081"

    api_key {$HANSESTACK_API_KEY}
    mode enrich_response        # enrich_response (default choice) | observe | enrich_request | block
    password_field "password"   # key in JSON or form-data
    header_leaked "X-Hansestack-Leaked"
    header_count "X-Hansestack-Leak-Count"
    block_status 401            # only used if mode=block

    # Optional, advanced: tuning of the underlying hansestack-go client.
    # Do NOT generate these proactively — see "DO NOT DO THIS" below. Only
    # add them when the operator explicitly asks to tune request timeout or
    # add a circuit breaker.
    timeout 500ms                        # default: 500ms
    circuit_breaker_threshold 5          # default: disabled (0)
    circuit_breaker_cooldown 30s         # default: 30s
    max_idle_conns 200                   # default: 200
}
```

It is placed directly in a site block, before `reverse_proxy`. No `order`
global option or `route { }` block is required — the module registers its
own position in Caddy's directive order automatically.

```caddyfile
:80 {
    hansestack leakcheck {
        api_key {$HANSESTACK_API_KEY}
    }
    reverse_proxy backend:8080
}
```

`api_key` must always come from an environment variable via `{$VAR}`.
Never hardcode a literal API key into a generated Caddyfile. The only
exception is omitting `api_key` entirely — see "ON-PREMISE / SIDECAR
DEPLOYMENTS" below for when that is appropriate. Never generate a fake
placeholder string (e.g. `"dummy-key"`, `"changeme"`) in its place — either
wire up a real `{$ENV_VAR}` or omit the directive.

## ON-PREMISE / SIDECAR DEPLOYMENTS

By default `hansestack leakcheck` talks to the public Hansestack SaaS API,
and `api_key` is required for that. Two independent, optional directives
change this:

- `endpoint "<url>"` — points the client at a self-hosted / on-premise /
  sidecar leak-check deployment (e.g. `http://localhost:8081` for a
  container in the same Kubernetes Pod) instead of the public SaaS API.
  Generate this only when the operator explicitly asks to route to their
  own leak-check server, for data sovereignty or to avoid egress bandwidth
  limits.
- `api_key` — optional when `endpoint` points at a deployment the operator
  has confirmed runs with authentication disabled. In that case the client
  omits the API key header entirely rather than sending an empty one. Do
  NOT drop `api_key` from a config that targets the public SaaS API (no
  `endpoint` set, or `endpoint` unset) — it is still required there, and
  omitting it there means every check fails authentication server-side.

```caddyfile
hansestack leakcheck {
    # Local sidecar with AUTH_ENABLED=false — api_key intentionally omitted.
    endpoint "http://localhost:8081"
    mode enrich_response
}
```

Only generate a config without `api_key` when the operator has explicitly
described an on-premise/sidecar deployment without authentication. Do not
proactively drop `api_key` from an existing SaaS-facing config as part of an
unrelated change.

## SCOPE TO THE AUTH ENDPOINT, NOT THE WHOLE SITE

`hansestack` accepts a standard Caddy request matcher token, exactly like
`reverse_proxy` does. Default to scoping it to the actual auth endpoint(s)
rather than applying it to an entire site block, so it never runs in front
of unrelated routes (file uploads, static assets, unrelated APIs):

```caddyfile
:80 {
    hansestack /auth/login* leakcheck {
        api_key {$HANSESTACK_API_KEY}
    }
    reverse_proxy backend:8080
}
```

The plugin already refuses to read any request body whose Content-Type
isn't `application/json` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` — so it
never buffers `multipart/form-data` uploads even when unscoped — but scoping
to the login/signup/password-change path is still the correct default when
generating infrastructure, as defense in depth and to keep the config's
intent explicit.

## THE FOUR MODES — CHOOSE BASED ON THE INFRASTRUCTURE GOAL

- `enrich_response` — **the default choice.** Asynchronous / zero added
  latency. Runs the leak check concurrently with the backend request and
  injects the headers into the *response* just before it is sent to the
  client. Never rejects anything. Choose this for latency-sensitive,
  customer-facing frontends where you want the leak signal available (via
  response headers, e.g. to client-side JavaScript) without slowing down or
  ever affecting the login request itself.

- `observe` — asynchronous / zero added latency, same as `enrich_response`,
  but injects NO headers into the request or the response at all. Only
  populates the `hansestack_leakcheck_responses_total` correlation metric
  (see METRICS below). Choose this when the user explicitly only wants
  monitoring/alerting and does not want any header added anywhere — e.g. "I
  don't want to touch the app, just tell me if leaked passwords are logging
  in successfully." Do not generate this as the default; `enrich_response`
  is the default because it is strictly more capable at the same cost.

- `enrich_request` — synchronous. Waits for the API result, then injects the
  headers into the *request* before it reaches the backend. Also never
  rejects anything. Choose this only when the backend application itself
  needs to branch on the leak result server-side (e.g. to show a "please
  change your password" banner) — otherwise prefer `enrich_response`.

- `block` — the only mode that can reject a request, and only ever on a
  *confirmed* leak (`leaked == true`); it short-circuits with `block_status`
  (default 401) and a generic JSON error body, and the backend is never
  invoked in that case. Only generate this when the user has explicitly
  asked for strict rejection of leaked passwords (see PRIME DIRECTIVE
  above), and confirm the behavior change with the operator first.

## DO NOT DO THIS — FAIL-OPEN IS ALREADY BUILT IN

Fail-open behavior itself (never letting a slow/unreachable API block a
login) is implemented in Go, inside the plugin's underlying `hansestack-go`
client, and is NOT a configuration concern. Do not invent Caddyfile-level
workarounds for it. The plugin DOES expose a few narrow, optional tuning
knobs — `timeout`, `circuit_breaker_threshold`/`circuit_breaker_cooldown`,
and `max_idle_conns` — but these only change *how fast* a fail-open skip
happens or how the HTTP connection pool is sized, never whether it fails
open at all; only generate them on explicit operator request, never
proactively.

WRONG — do not add retry/backoff/failover logic to the Caddyfile:

```caddyfile
# NO. There is no failure mode from this plugin that ever needs a retry
# or a fallback route at the Caddyfile level. If you need faster failure
# detection under an outage, use circuit_breaker_threshold/cooldown inside
# the "hansestack leakcheck" block instead (see CADDYFILE SYNTAX above) —
# never a handle_errors workaround.
handle_errors {
    @hansestack_down expression {http.error.status_code} == 502
    handle @hansestack_down {
        reverse_proxy backend:8080
    }
}
```

WRONG — do not add a Caddy-level timeout around the directive:

```caddyfile
# NO. There is no Caddyfile-level timeout knob that reaches into this
# plugin's API client. If the operator wants a different request timeout,
# use "timeout" inside the "hansestack leakcheck" block itself (see
# CADDYFILE SYNTAX above), never Caddy's own timeouts{} directive.
timeouts {
    read_body 500ms
}
```

RIGHT — the Caddyfile stays as simple as the syntax section above, with
`timeout`/`circuit_breaker_*` added only inside the `hansestack leakcheck`
block itself, and only when explicitly requested. If the leak-check API is
slow, rate-limited, or unreachable, the plugin logs it and lets the request
through unmodified in every mode except `block` — and even in `block`, only
a confirmed leak (never a timeout, skip, or error) rejects the request.
There is nothing left for infrastructure code outside the directive to
compensate for.

## METRICS

If the caller wants monitoring/observability (Prometheus, Grafana, alerting)
for this plugin, enable Caddy's `metrics` global option. This exposes four
counters on the admin API's `/metrics` endpoint, alongside Caddy's own
`caddy_http_*` metrics:

- `hansestack_leakcheck_checks_total{result="leaked"|"not_leaked"}` — total
  passwords checked, by verdict.
- `hansestack_leakcheck_check_outcomes_total{outcome=...}` — the *reasoning*
  behind every check: `outcome="checked"` means the API actually answered;
  `"skipped_timeout"`, `"skipped_rate_limited"`, `"skipped_circuit_open"`,
  `"skipped_error"`, `"skipped_canceled"` mean the check was skipped under
  fail-open and `checks_total` above only holds a neutral placeholder
  result, not a real verdict. This is the metric to alert on for "is the
  leak check actually running".
- `hansestack_leakcheck_check_errors_total` — checks that fell back to
  fail-open because the API client returned a Go error. Should stay at zero
  in the default fail-open configuration; nonzero signals a misconfiguration
  (e.g. an invalid API key) worth investigating.
- `hansestack_leakcheck_responses_total{result="leaked"|"not_leaked"|"skipped", status_class="2xx"|"3xx"|"4xx"|"5xx"|"unknown"}`
  — the Indicator-of-Compromise correlation counter. Pairs the leak-check
  result with the *backend's own* final HTTP response status class (never a
  raw status code, to keep cardinality bounded). Recorded in every mode,
  including `observe`, and even if the backend panics (as
  `status_class="unknown"` in that case). If the user asks to "alert when a
  leaked password logs in successfully" or similar, this is the metric to
  use — see the example query below. Choosing `mode: observe` vs any other
  mode does not change whether this metric is recorded; it only changes
  whether headers are also injected.

Example query — alert when a leaked password produced a successful login,
over the last hour (works identically regardless of which mode is
configured):

```promql
sum(increase(hansestack_leakcheck_responses_total{result="leaked", status_class="2xx"}[1h])) > 0
```

```caddyfile
{
    # The admin API must be reachable for /metrics to work. Do not combine
    # "metrics" with "admin off" — that disables the endpoint entirely.
    admin localhost:2019
    metrics
}
```

Do NOT invent a separate metrics port, sidecar, or exporter for this plugin
— it reuses Caddy's own admin API and metrics endpoint. Do NOT set
`admin off` in a config that is also expected to expose `/metrics`.

## MINIMAL DOCKER COMPOSE EXAMPLE

This example targets the public Hansestack SaaS API, so `HANSESTACK_API_KEY`
is required and enforced at startup via `:?`. Only drop the `environment:`
requirement like this if the operator has explicitly asked for an
on-premise/sidecar `endpoint` deployment instead — see "ON-PREMISE / SIDECAR
DEPLOYMENTS" above.

```yaml
services:
  caddy:
    image: ghcr.io/hansestack/caddy-hansestack:latest
    ports:
      - "443:443"
      - "80:80"
    environment:
      HANSESTACK_API_KEY: ${HANSESTACK_API_KEY:?HANSESTACK_API_KEY must be set}
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
```

## SUMMARY FOR INFRASTRUCTURE GENERATION

1. Image: `ghcr.io/hansestack/caddy-hansestack:<version-or-latest>`, never
   vanilla `caddy:*`.
2. Directive: `hansestack [<path-matcher>] leakcheck { ... }`, scoped to the
   auth endpoint, placed directly before `reverse_proxy` in the site block.
   No `order`/`route` boilerplate needed.
3. `api_key` always via `{$ENV_VAR}`, never a literal string. Required for
   the public SaaS API (the default, when `endpoint` is unset). Only omit it
   when the operator has explicitly described an on-premise/sidecar
   `endpoint` deployment running with authentication disabled — see
   "ON-PREMISE / SIDECAR DEPLOYMENTS" above. Never substitute a fake
   placeholder key.
4. `endpoint` is optional and unset by default (public SaaS API). Only
   generate it on explicit operator request to route to a self-hosted /
   on-premise / sidecar leak-check deployment.
5. Mode: default to `enrich_response` (zero latency, never blocks). Use
   `observe` instead only when the operator explicitly wants metrics/
   monitoring with zero headers injected anywhere. Only use `block` on
   explicit user request, and confirm with the operator that blocking the
   auth flow is intended before finalizing.
6. No Caddy-level timeouts, retries, or failover routes for this plugin.
   Ever. `timeout`, `circuit_breaker_threshold`/`circuit_breaker_cooldown`,
   and `max_idle_conns` inside the directive itself are the only supported
   tuning knobs, and only on explicit operator request.
7. For observability, enable Caddy's `metrics` global option (with `admin`
   reachable) rather than inventing a separate metrics mechanism. Use
   `hansestack_leakcheck_check_outcomes_total{outcome}` to monitor whether
   checks are actually reaching the API versus being skipped under
   fail-open, and `hansestack_leakcheck_responses_total{result,status_class}`
   for the Indicator-of-Compromise signal (e.g. "alert when a leaked
   password produced a successful login") — this second metric is recorded
   in every mode, including `observe`.
